#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when a specific version must never appear*
This scenario demonstrates how to stop a version from entering the build in sbt, which has no `reject` keyword but does have a mechanism that fails the build when resolution would upgrade across an incompatible boundary.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
The eviction error (`libraryDependencySchemes`, `evictionErrorLevel`) arrived in **sbt 1.5**. Before that, sbt only warned.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibB1[lib-b:1.0.0]
    Root --> LibA[lib-a:2.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB2[lib-b:2.0.0]
    LibB1 -. "evicted by 2.0.0: incompatible under early-semver" .-> X((build fails))
```

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="s14-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
I can list a bad version and the build tool refuses to resolve it, the way Gradle's `reject` does.

#### ! Actual
sbt has no version blacklist. What it has, since 1.5, is a compatibility check on evictions: declare the version scheme a library follows, and when conflict resolution would replace one version with an incompatible one, `update` fails. Here `lib-b:1.0.0` would be evicted by `2.0.0`; under early-semver a major bump is incompatible, so sbt stops with "found version conflict(s) in library dependencies; some are suspected to be binary incompatible". With `evictionErrorLevel := Level.Warn` the same build resolves `lib-b:2.0.0` and merely warns.

#### ! Why
Gradle rejects a *version*; sbt rejects an *incompatible upgrade*. The check runs after resolution: for every evicted artifact, sbt compares the loser and the winner under the declared scheme (`early-semver`, `semver-spec`, `pvp`, `strict`, or `always`) and raises an error if the pair is incompatible. Scala libraries can publish their scheme in the POM (`versionScheme`), and `libraryDependencySchemes` lets you declare it for libraries that do not. Plain Java artifacts are assumed `always` compatible unless you say otherwise, which is why the build file declares one for `lib-b`.

#### ! Fix
*   **Fix the graph:** upgrade the direct `lib-b` to `2.0.0`, or hold `lib-a` at `1.0.0`, so nothing incompatible is evicted. This is the right answer when the error is telling the truth.
*   **Pin with `dependencyOverrides`:** force `lib-b` to the version you need (SB6). The check still runs on the eviction, so pair it with the next option if you have verified compatibility.
*   **Override the check consciously:** `ThisBuild / evictionErrorLevel := Level.Warn`, or declare `libraryDependencySchemes += "com.demo" % "lib-b" % VersionScheme.Always` for a library you know is compatible across the jump. Comment it.
*   **Blacklist specific versions:** sbt has no native way. A small custom task that inspects `update.value.allModules` and fails on a banned coordinate, or a CI grep over `sbt dependencyTree`, provides it.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Declaring version schemes for the libraries you depend on and letting the check guard upgrades.
* MEDIUM Setting `evictionErrorLevel` to `Warn` globally to silence one false positive, and losing the guard for every library.
* HIGH Using `VersionScheme.Always` on a library that is not in fact always compatible; the check passes, the runtime does not.

#### ! Control
Keep `libraryDependencySchemes` and any `evictionErrorLevel` change in one commented block. Make a CI job fail on the eviction error rather than warn, and treat each override of the check as a reviewed decision.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `sbt update`, then `sbt -Dsb14.allow=true "show externalDependencyClasspath"`

**What to look for:** The first command fails with the binary-incompatibility error naming `lib-b`. The second succeeds, warns, and shows `lib-b-2.0.0.jar` on the classpath.

**Conclusion:** sbt cannot reject a version by name, but it can refuse an incompatible eviction, and you choose whether that refusal is an error or a warning.

#### ! Scales
Version rejection is critical for security compliance: when a CVE lands on a specific release, teams need assurance that it cannot appear anywhere in the graph. In sbt that assurance comes from `dependencyOverrides` pins plus a CI assertion, with the eviction check guarding against the opposite failure, an upgrade that silently breaks binary compatibility.

#### ! Takeaway
sbt rejects incompatible evictions, not named versions. Declare schemes, keep the error level at `Error`, and pin plus verify when you need a real blacklist.

#### ! Wild

When sbt 1.5 shipped the eviction error in 2021, thousands of builds broke on the same library: `scala-xml`. Scala 2.13 tooling pulled `scala-xml` 2.x while older plugins and libraries still asked for 1.x, the library declared early-semver, and sbt correctly refused the major-version eviction. The workaround that spread through the community, `ThisBuild / libraryDependencySchemes += "org.scala-lang.modules" %% "scala-xml" % VersionScheme.Always`, is exactly the "override the check consciously" option above, and it is still in a great many build files today.
